newsitem.title: BURUNDI: 250 killed in Burundi army attacks, residents say.
newsitem.headline: 250 killed in Burundi army attacks, residents say.

text.p: Residents of Buchaganzwa in eastern Burundi said on Sunday that 250 civilians were killed with guns and bayonets when the Burundi army launched attacks aimed at armed Hutu rebels there last month.
Travellers from the area who arrived in Bujumbura at the weekend said the massacre on November 15 caused thousands to flee across the border into neighbouring Tanzania.
"Many of those killed were women, children and old men. They were herded into a valley and killed. This massacre caused people to flee from their homes," one traveller said.
"Officials said 3,000 had crossed into Tanzania," the traveller said, adding that other sources put the figure much higher.
Residents said at least 250 people were killed in the attacks.
Officials in Bujumbura said on Sunday that only 19 people were killed in army operations in the area last month.

The Burundi government on Saturday denied a report by the London-based Amnesty International that its Tutsi-led security forces had killed at least 1,000 unarmed Hutu civilians in the past month, some while sheltering in churches.
"We refute the allegations completely," Jean-Luc Ndizeye, spokesman for President Pierre Buyoya told Reuters.

Amnesty said on Friday that up to 500 people were massacred in the Pentecostal Church of Nyarurama on December 3. Nyarurama is 60 km (40 miles) southeast of Bujumbura and about the same distance from Buchaganzwa.

The victims had been told that they could shelter safely in the church but, once they were inside, soldiers surrounded the building, threw grenades inside and shot at or bayoneted those trying to escape, Amnesty said in a news release.
Then the troops set the church on fire, sought out those who had escaped and killed them as well.
But Ndizeye said that rebel activity was prevalent in the area Amnesty International spoke of and "there have been casualties in such areas, this everyone knows".

Hundreds of thousands of people, mainly Hutus, have died in tribal conflict in Burundi over the last 25 years -- at least 150,000 of them in violence following the murder in 1993 of the country's first Hutu president, Melchior Ndadaye.
